docs.text:
Welcome to the Delta Simulations Documentation Hub, for any and all information about our projects

You Should Know

The documentation provided is a Work in Progress, and may feature incomplete information. Please refer to our Discord for the most up-to-date information.

  • UH-60M Blackhawk

    The UH-60 Blackhawk is a four-bladed, twin-engine, medium-lift utility helicopter manufactured by Sikorsky Aircraft.

  • C-17A Globemaster III Documentation Coming Soon

    The C-17A Globemaster III is a large military transport aircraft developed by McDonnell Douglas (now Boeing). It's capable of rapid strategic delivery of troops and cargo to main operating bases or forward operating bases.

    The KC-46A Pegasus is a military aerial refueling and strategic military transport aircraft developed by Boeing.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If the above methods do not work:

To find the Community folder that MSFS is using, please follow these steps:

  1. Go to your General Settings in MSFS and activate Developer Mode.
  2. Go to the menu and select 'Virtual File System'.
  3. Click on 'Packages Folders' and select 'Open Community Folder'. This opens the Community folder in a Windows Explorer. Please ensure that your add-ons are installed in the folder that is opened.

docs.text: If you would like to manually perform a clean install you have to delete the deltasimulations-XXX folder from your community folder.

docs.title: How do I report an issue?
docs.text:
CHECK THIS FIRST

We highly recommend joining Our Discord for the fastest response time. Alternatively, please submit a Github Issue on the relevant repo containing the aircraft version, simulator version, and specific, reproducible steps to achieve this issue. Please be as specific as possible.

docs.title: Before Reporting Issues
docs.text:
Please try removing all other mods/liveries from the community folder and test our add-on again. We also reccomend doing a clean install. This will help rule out conflicts.

Most reported issues are caused by conflicts with other mods and liveries, or from an incorrect installation. If this does not resolve your issue, please continue below.

docs.title: How Can I Support Development?
docs.text:
If you are looking to assist with the development, you can start immediately with a PR or fork on our Github, though we highly recommend first filling out our Team Application Form so we can onboard you onto our server, and you can gain access to our reference libraries.

As a freeware organization, we rely on self-funding to cover the software, equipment, and subscriptions required to develop our projects. After years of development and thousands of dollars personally invested, we’re working to make the group more sustainable for the long term.

Donations are the most effective way to support our work if you are not a developer:

Donate via PayPal

Supporters receive a special role on our Discord server along with sneak peeks and additional updates on our development progress. If you donate, please contact a moderator on Discord with proof of donation to receive your role.

Please note: donations do not provide early access to any of our projects — only additional development updates and behind-the-scenes information.

docs.title: Will These Projects Be Available on Xbox?
docs.text: These projects are PC-only at this time, and will remain so for the foreseable future.

docs.title: When I Click a Button/Test, It Doesn't Work as it Should
docs.text: Our aircraft code runs on the PC-based XML scripting which is much easier to debug and adapt for complex aircraft. As a result, you may run into interaction issues when using the XBOX/LOCK control modes. We design our aircraft for use in the LEGACY control mode

docs.title: Are These Projects Free?
docs.text: Yes! This is the heart of our philosophy - our aircrafts will forever be free, open-source, and available to all. We will never gatekeep products behind paywalls or limited access. What you see is what you get.

docs.title: When is the Next Update?
docs.text: We are a team of volunteers developing in our free time and are thus unable to provide an estimate for a release date. We believe in releasing "beta" test builds of our aircraft, allowing for an effective feedback loop. When we believe we have a stable enough build, we will post it in our Discord, and it will be available on Github under the aircraft's releases. Then, you can follow our download instructions available above.

docs.title: UH-60M Black Hawk
docs.text: Pilot documentation for the Delta Simulations H-60 family in Microsoft Flight Simulator.

docs.title: First flight
docs.text:
1. Install the aircraft and select a variant.
  2. Set up the cyclic, collective and pedals. The keybinds guide lists the aircraft's special assignments.
  3. Follow the quick start or begin at the full before-start checklist.
  4. Fly a short departure, cruise and arrival, then use parking and shutdown.

docs.title: Primary flight controls
docs.text:
Assign cyclic longitudinal, cyclic lateral, collective and tail rotor to continuous axes. On a throttle quadrant used as a collective, select the collective axis. If both pedals and a twist grip control yaw, keep the assignment on the device you intend to fly with.

Use Helicopter Controller Profiles for the full setup, Axis Calibration and Troubleshooting for reversed or competing inputs, and Exterior Lights and Searchlight to check the light movement from outside.

For a first flight, follow the cockpit walkthrough. For controller setup, aircraft loading and flight planning, see the full UH-60M Pilot Handbook.

docs.title: Cockpit Displays
docs.text:
For departure, keep a PFD in front of the flying seat and EICAS on the next screen. When you want the route, select ND on the adjacent display. Each screen retains its own page selection. If only one stays dark, start with that display's PWR switch.

What you need to read Instrument Attitude, barometric altitude and selected heading Primary flight display Command bars, FD1 and selected reference Flight director and mode selectors Torque, rotor speed and fuel EICAS engine and rotor indications Why a message appears EICAS crew alerts Flight-plan leg or moving map ND and flight plan · Moving map controls Drift over a landing spot HUD hover cue Second attitude or height reference Standby instruments · Barometric and radar altitude

For individual bezel selections, including JMVF and IVHMS, use the multifunction display page list.

docs.title: Batteries and generators
docs.text: The batteries provide power before a generator is online. On the overhead panel, BATT NO. 1 and BATT NO. 2 control the batteries. The two engine generators and the APU generator each have a separate switch.

docs.title: Flight control hydraulics
docs.text:
Hydraulic pressure assists the flight controls. The BACKUP HYD PUMP switch belongs to the hydraulic system. The nearby fuel pump switches serve the engines and APU.

The Before Start checklist gives the initial switch positions. The Cockpit Equipment Checks cover the next part of the startup.

docs.title: When a panel goes dark
docs.text: Start with the extent of the problem. One dark MFD with a working neighbor points to that screen's power selection. Several dark displays and silent radios call for a look at the main electrical supply. The electrical bus and generator guide identifies the main, hot battery and essential avionics circuits. The standby instrument has its own battery selection.

docs.title: When several hydraulic messages appear together
docs.text: The parked leak test drives a group of reservoir, pump and servo messages from one test state. Moving the switch from TEST back to NORM leaves the state latched. The hydraulic test guide covers RESET and lists the expected messages by area of the screen. Compare any remaining message with the EICAS caution list.

docs.title: Cyclic, Collective and Pedals
docs.text:
Set up these axes in your MSFS helicopter controls profile. The pilot and copilot have the same primary controls.

Cockpit control Axis What it does Cyclic Pitch and roll Tilts the rotor disc forward, aft, left or right. Collective Collective Changes the pitch of all main rotor blades together. Pedals Yaw Changes tail rotor thrust to swing the nose left or right.

Move one control at a time and watch the matching control in the cockpit. If the nose turns the wrong way when you press a pedal, check the direction of the yaw axis in your profile.

SAS is the stability augmentation system. It damps unwanted motion. You'll also see TRIM and FPS (flight path stabilization) in the cockpit equipment checks.

docs.title: Setup and flight guidance
docs.text:
Assign cyclic pitch and roll, collective, and a single yaw axis on your helicopter controller profile. If the cockpit pedals jump back as soon as you release them, check for another yaw assignment on a twist stick or gamepad. To isolate that input before changing sensitivity, use axis calibration and troubleshooting.

SAS, FPS and rotor trim affect a different part of the control setup from flight director and mode selection. The PFD can display a director command while the pilot still flies the maneuver.

docs.title: Multifunction Display Pages
docs.text:
Use the bottom bezel to choose what appears on each screen. A screen set to PFD can stay in that format while another shows the route or engine indications. Look for JMVF on the bezel and LOAD DTS beside its on-screen load key.

Page Selection What appears PFD Press PFD. Attitude, heading, indicated airspeed, altitude and vertical speed. PFD indications ND Press ND. Compass and simulator flight-plan waypoints. Navigation display EICAS Press EICAS. Engine and rotor indications, fuel quantities, cautions and advisories. Engine instruments TAC Press TAC. Moving map with scale, orientation and centering controls. Moving map JMVF Press JMVF. Waypoint-data load key and DTS status. Data transfer IVHMS From EICAS, press EICAS again. Administration page with aircraft identification, version and DTS status. Press EICAS again to return. Aircraft status

If the bezel lettering is visible but the screen is dark, check that display's PWR switch and the shared backlight. See display power and bezel keys.

docs.title: Engines, Fuel and APU
docs.text: The UH-60M has two T700-GE-701D turboshaft engines. Select EICAS on a multifunction display to see the engine and rotor indications together.

docs.title: Fuel system
docs.text: The helicopter carries fuel in two main tanks. Each engine has its own fuel feed. On the overhead panel, the engine boost pump switches are separate from the FUEL PUMP selector used for APU boost.

docs.title: Auxiliary power unit
docs.text:
The APU supplies electrical power on the ground and bleed air for engine start. The APU CONT switch controls the unit. The APU generator switch controls its electrical output.

For the switch sequence in the sim, see Starting Engines.

docs.title: Read the panel during a start
docs.text:
Look for APU ON and APU GEN ON separately. A running APU can supply bleed air with its generator disconnected. Follow the air-source and ground-power controls when one source appears available but another does not.

Use the power control lever guide for the modeled detents. Compare Q, NG, TGT, NP and NR by label. The PFD's two torque indications use separate engine inputs, while both sets of EICAS engine tapes read engine 1.

For a fuel check, read the quantities in both main tanks before and after a timed leg. Use total fuel consumed by both engines for cruise endurance.

docs.title: Military Models
docs.text:
UH-60M · MikeHH-60M · DustoffHH-60W · Jolly Green IIHH-60U · Ghost HawkMH-60M · Night StalkerMH-60M · DAP

A base "Mike" model with UES, advanced flight control system, and upgraded rotor blades. Standard configuration for troop transport and utility missions. Also simulated is a HIRSS equipped Mike model.

2 Pilots + 2 Crew with dedicated medical evacuation configuration, including integrated patient treatment system, equipped with an external rescue hoist.

The US Air Force's newest Combat Search and Rescue (CSAR) helicopter featuring increased fuel capacity, advanced defensive systems, and improved armor protection for personnel recovery missions.

A byproduct of a test cycle, these rarely seen aircraft are used as a testbed for Skunkworks UH-60M modifications and security of the Groom Lake area.

Piloted exclusively by the U.S. Army's 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment (SOAR), also known as the Night Stalkers, this special operations variant is equipped with several advanced sensors and capabilities to allow clandestine operations.

The DAP - Direct Action Penetrator, is the weaponised variant of the 160th's MH-60M. Using external stores, it can be equipped with several weapons platforms.

docs.title: Finding a cockpit indication
docs.text: Use the label beside the reading to choose a page. NR is rotor speed, RA is height above terrain, and REF identifies the selected display reference. For a message that appeared during a test, look up its exact wording under crew alerts.

docs.title: Cabin, Hoist and Utility Equipment
docs.text:
Cabin equipment depends on which H-60 you select in MSFS.

Variant Equipment UH-60M “Mike” Utility cabin for passengers and cargo. HH-60M “Dustoff” Medical cabin with a patient treatment system and an external rescue hoist. S-70i “Helitak” Firefighting tank. The Keybinds Guide lists its release binding under Bambi/Helitak Release.

The Variants page has photos of the different configurations. Use the cockpit tablet’s Aircraft tab to see which fittings the selected model supports.

docs.title: Configuring a rescue or firefighting flight
docs.text:
Start with the full aircraft title in the variant guide. A repaint can supply a medical paint scheme while retaining the utility cabin. On a stock HH-60M Medevac, open Aircraft on the tablet and look at the hoist and door controls. The equipment guide identifies the moving doors, crew visibility switches and variant-specific fittings.

On the S-70i Helitak, check the water-system indication before assigning a release control. The firefighting equipment guide distinguishes the fixed belly tank from the bucket. Set passenger and cargo weights in MSFS payload stations separately from the visible cabin configuration.

The data page reads JMVF on the bezel and LOAD DTS beside the on-screen key. The status flag records a load request. For missing markers, check the data transfer page. For missing route legs, check the MSFS flight plan.

The lamp test exercises the warning panel. The hydraulic leak test has its own switch and reset. After the cockpit checks, continue with Starting Engines.

docs.title: Landing
docs.text:
• Roll-on landing

    A roll-on landing may be used when the helicopter will not sustain a hover or to avoid hovering in snow or dust

  • Slope landing

    The tailwheel should be locked and the parking brake should be set. For slope landings and all ground operations, avoid using combinations of excessive cyclic and low collective settings.

docs.title: Reading the instruments on final
docs.text:
Use a fixed point on the landing area to check drift. The HUD hover cue shows forward and sideways motion relative to the aircraft. The PFD digital airspeed window has a 30-knot floor. It can still say 30 on the ground.

At an elevated airport the barometric altimeter continues to show field elevation after touchdown. Use the radar altitude indication to compare height over the landing surface. At the stand, continue with parking and shutdown.

docs.title: Before ending the simulator session
docs.text:
During rundown, compare the NR indication with the rotor brake lever. Wheel braking, tailwheel lock and rotor braking use separate controls. If the helicopter moves after parking, record whether the wheels rolled, the tailwheel pivoted, or only the blades kept turning.

For an unexpected cockpit state on your next load, check whether you selected a parking spot or an airborne start. The start-state table lists what the two presets initialize.

docs.text:
The H-60 features a rudimentary weapons system for the MH-60M and HH-60W models. Arm the weapons via either the EFB, or the DISP ARM switch on the center console. The weapons can then be fired via either the keybindable trigger or the EFB Aircraft Menu.

docs.title: Cabin Heating and Ventilation
docs.text: Several controls can affect airflow in a UH-60M cockpit. The HEATER changes the temperature of the air sent through the ducts. The VENT BLOWER circulates ambient air. Adjustable nozzles near the consoles let the pilots direct ram air where they want it.

docs.title: Heat source and airflow
docs.text:
The basic heating system mixes outside air with hot compressed air taken from an engine compressor. The latter is called bleed air. The APU can also supply it on the ground. The mixing system regulates the temperature delivered to the cabin and cockpit outlets. By contrast, the electric ventilation blower moves ambient air through the cabin ducts even when no heat is selected.

The AIR SCE HT/STRT label in Delta's Before Start checklist means air source for heat and start. The selector identifies the pneumatic source. The separate heater control sets the heat delivered to the occupants. This explains why the air-source selector also appears in the add-on's engine runup checklist.

docs.title: Cabin equipment varies
docs.text:
An AUX CABIN HEATER panel identifies supplemental cabin heat. In a medical cabin equipped with an environmental control system (ECS), a separate panel near the medic seat controls cooling and recirculation.

The documented simulator interaction is the air-source selector in the linked checklists. The auxiliary heater, rear-cabin ECS and temperature response depend on what the selected add-on variant implements.

docs.title: Main and Tail Rotors
docs.text: Two details to look for in an exterior view are the four blades above the cabin and the angle of the tail rotor. On the UH-60M, both rotors receive power from the transmission, and each changes blade pitch in response to the flight controls.

docs.title: Main rotor head
docs.text:
The four main blades meet at a central hub. Pitch is the angle of a blade about its long axis. The swashplate and pitch links change that angle as the blades turn. The hub also lets each blade move up or down (flap) and move slightly forward or back in the plane of rotation (lead or lag). These are different motions from changing blade pitch.

When the rotor is stationary, droop stops support the blades. This accounts for the difference in blade position between a parked aircraft and one carrying its weight on the rotor. A vibration absorber at the rotor head reduces vibration transmitted to the fuselage.

docs.title: Tail rotor
docs.text: The tail rotor sits on the right side of the raised tail pylon. The tilt is intentional. Most of its thrust acts sideways to counter the turning effect of the main rotor and control yaw. Because its thrust is angled, a part of it also supports the helicopter's weight in a hover.

docs.title: Vibration in the cockpit
docs.text: The airframe has a separate active vibration control system. It senses rotor-induced vibration in the aircraft and generates an opposing vibration. The VIB CONT switch in Delta's Before Start checklist refers to this system. The checklist identifies the cockpit control. Camera shake or force feedback alone cannot tell you how much of the system your add-on models.

docs.title: Rotor Brake and Rundown
docs.text: The rotor brake acts on the revolving drive system. The parking brake acts at the wheels, and the tailwheel lock limits wheel swivel. Each has a separate cockpit control. On an exterior view the helicopter can sit perfectly still while the blades are still turning.

docs.title: Reading the shutdown indications
docs.text:
Keep EICAS in view for the engine and rotor portion of the parking and shutdown checklist. Watch the NR indication as the rotor slows. The checklist gives the sim's rotor-brake point as at or below 40% NR. Use the instrument for that reading. At some frame rates the exterior blade animation can look almost stationary while the rotor is still turning.

The cockpit rotor brake has two tooltip states, ROTOR BRAKE (UNLOCKED) and ROTOR BRAKE (ENGAGED). Clicking the lever toggles the aircraft's local brake selection. While that selection is engaged, the model repeatedly sends the simulator's rotor-brake-on command. The lever animation reads the simulator's active brake state.

docs.title: A brake that appears to reapply itself
docs.text:
If an external controller releases the brake for an instant and the lever returns to engaged, click the cockpit lever to unlock it and check the tooltip again. A generic controller release can conflict with the cockpit's retained selection. On the next parked session, compare the same cockpit action with the controller disconnected or its rotor brake assignment temporarily cleared.

If the wheels roll with the rotor stopped, check the parking brake and tailwheel lock. An unlocked tailwheel permits swivel while moving. It cannot hold a parked helicopter in place. When reporting an apparent brake fault, identify which object moved: blades, wheels, or the tailwheel pivot.

Cockpit rotor-brake lever · Engine and rotor indications

docs.title: Standby Flight Instruments
docs.text: The Electronic Standby Instrument System (ESIS) gives the pilots a compact second view of the aircraft's attitude and motion. The standby system has its own display and backup battery. It can display pitch, roll, airspeed, altitude, vertical speed and heading independently of the selected multifunction display page.

docs.title: Read the standby picture
docs.text: Indication How to interpret it Attitude The fixed aircraft reference and moving horizon show pitch and bank. The roll pointer reads against the scale above them. Airspeed, altitude and vertical speed The standby air data computer uses pressure from the pitot-static system. The BARO setting provides the pressure reference for displayed altitude. When comparing the main and standby altitudes in the sim, first check that their pressure settings match. Heading Read the heading tape at its fixed center index. The standby system has a magnetic sensor to supply this information.

docs.title: Other visual references
docs.text: Look above the instrument panel on the right center windshield frame for the separate magnetic compass. A panel clock offers clock time (C) and elapsed time (ET). Two direct-reading indicators in the overhead windows show outside air temperature in degrees Celsius. These references can help identify instruments in cockpit views where only their labels are legible.

docs.title: The add-on's standby check
docs.text: Delta's Before Start checklist identifies the battery check indication as BATT GOOD and calls out the ESIS tone during the standby instrument check. The Cockpit Equipment Checks list the STBY INST switch again. Use the switch position and BATT GOOD indication together when checking standby power on the ramp.

docs.title: Transmission and Tail Drive
docs.text: The UH-60M has two engines and one main rotor. Each engine feeds its own input module on the main transmission above the cabin. The main transmission brings the two inputs together, reduces their speed and turns the main rotor mast. A second drive takes power aft to the tail rotor.

docs.title: Follow the power through the aircraft
docs.text: Component What it drives Main transmission The main rotor above the cabin and the drive shaft leading into the tail. Accessory modules A generator and a hydraulic pump on each side. This mechanical connection helps explain why generator indications change as the rotor comes up to speed. Intermediate gearbox The next section of the tail drive at the bend near the base of the tail pylon. Tail gearbox The tail rotor at the top of the pylon. Its gears turn the drive through the final change in direction.

docs.title: Read the indications
docs.text:
In the add-on's engine runup checklist, Q1 and Q2 refer to the torque supplied by each engine. NR refers to the speed of their shared main rotor. Two torque indications and one rotor speed are what you would expect from this arrangement.

XMSN on a cockpit label stands for transmission. MAIN XMSN labels refer to the main gearbox oil. Engine oil belongs to a separate system. On EICAS, the MAIN XMSN PRESS message follows modeled rotor speed. See crew alerts and test indications for the inputs behind the cockpit messages.

docs.title: Windshield and Pitot Heat
docs.text:
The windshield wipers, heated glass and heated pitot probes serve three different purposes. A wiper clears water that is already on the glass. Windshield heat acts on the glass itself. Pitot heat acts on the external probes that supply pressure information to the flight instruments.

Cockpit label What it refers to WINDSHIELD WIPER One motor drives a wiper on each pilot's windshield. LOW and HI select wiping speeds. OFF stops the blades where they are. PARK returns them to the inboard windshield frames. WINDSHIELD ANTI-ICE Transparent electrical conductors heat the glass for anti-icing and defogging. The pilot, copilot and center panes have individual switches. The center pane can therefore have its own heat control even though it has no wiper. PITOT HEAT Heating elements in the external pitot probes help keep their pressure openings clear of ice. The two probes sit behind and above the cockpit doors.

A moving wiper is a visible mechanical effect. Pitot heat has no comparable effect on the windshield. If you're looking around the virtual cockpit, the separate controls explain why a clear windshield tells you little about what the probes are sensing. For the instruments that use those pressure inputs, see Standby Flight Instruments.

In the simulator, either pilot’s pitot heat selection commands MSFS pitot heat. Wiper movement shows the blade position. It gives no indication of probe temperature or glass heating.

docs.title: COM Radios and Audio Selection
docs.text: COM1 and COM2 each have an active frequency and a standby frequency in the Delta H-60. The active frequency determines which station you can hear. The transmit selector determines which radio carries your voice. You can tune COM2 correctly and still transmit on COM1.

docs.title: Tune a radio
docs.text:
1. Bring the helicopter's electrical system online. If the cockpit is dark, use the electrical power guide before troubleshooting the audio.
  2. On a hardware radio panel or in your MSFS controls, select COM1 or COM2. Set the standby frequency. The whole-number and fractional controls adjust different parts of the frequency.
  3. Transfer standby to active on that same radio. Check the digits again after transfer. On a panel that shows both frequencies, the old active frequency should now appear in standby.
  4. Select the desired radio for transmit. Set the receive selector and audio output so you can hear it. Listening to a second frequency leaves the original transmit selection in place.

The add-on declares two COM radios with standby tuning. Several keys on the modeled pedestal keypad have no cockpit action. If a keypad press has no effect, use the corresponding MSFS COM command or a radio panel that reads the simulator's active frequency.

docs.title: Flying on VATSIM with vPilot
docs.text:
Set your headset output, microphone and push-to-talk button in vPilot. Speak at normal volume and check the microphone meter in its audio settings. Then compare vPilot's frequency and transmit selection with your intended station before calling.

In the vPilot message box Result .com1 FREQUENCY or .com2 FREQUENCY Tunes the named radio. Substitute the frequency published for the station. .com 1 or .com 2 Selects the radio used for transmit. .com both Toggles reception on both radios. Check the receive indicators after using it.

For a handoff, leave the current controller on COM1, tune the next controller on COM2, then switch transmit when instructed. If you can hear the new controller but they cannot hear you, check which radio has TX before changing the frequency again. If the TX selection is correct, check push-to-talk and the microphone meter separately.

docs.title: Moving Map and Route Entry
docs.text: To put a route on the ND, set the departure, destination and any intermediate waypoints in the simulator flight planner before loading the flight. Select ND and look for the line between the first two waypoints. The pedestal DIR key has no assigned click action. Pressing it will not create a direct-to leg on the map.

docs.title: Three ways to look at the route
docs.text:
Display What it shows When to use it ND Heading, waypoint identifiers and lines joining the simulator flight-plan positions. Trace the order of the legs or find the next turn. TAC A moving map with orientation, scale, centering and symbol controls. Match the helicopter's position to nearby map features. Cockpit tablet Map A separate map on the aircraft tablet. Keep a map open while the two front displays show flight and engine instruments.

On the moving map, ORIENT shows NORTH or HDG. In north-up the map holds its orientation while the aircraft symbol rotates. In heading-up the aircraft stays pointed up and the map rotates underneath it. If the line to the destination appears sideways after changing orientation, compare the waypoint names first. The change affects the picture, not the leg sequence.

MAP CTR selects a centered or offset presentation. The offset gives more room in front of the aircraft. ZOOM changes the area you see, and DECL changes how much symbology is drawn. When an expected feature goes missing, restore a wider scale and check declutter before editing the route.

docs.title: Check an empty map
docs.text:
Start a short flight between two airports you know. First find the two airport identifiers on the ND. If only one waypoint is available, there is no leg to join. Switch to the moving map and locate the aircraft on the ramp. Change one setting at a time so you can distinguish a change in scale from a change in orientation. Extra markers loaded through JMVF are separate from the route. See data transfer and aircraft status.

Moving map display · Map labels · Pedestal key bindings

docs.title: Navigation Receivers and Transponder
docs.text: The aircraft configuration supplies two NAV receivers, an ADF receiver, a marker beacon receiver and one transponder. The moving map gets its route from the simulator flight plan. Changing a radio frequency leaves that route in place.

docs.title: NAV1 and NAV2
docs.text:
Both NAV receivers have standby tuning. NAV1 is configured for a glideslope signal. NAV2 is configured without glideslope. For an offline receiver check, choose a station from the simulator's navigation data, tune the standby frequency on the intended receiver and transfer it to active. If you use a hardware panel, verify both the NAV receiver number and the active window. COM tuning on the same hardware controls a different pair of radios.

Receiving a signal, displaying its guidance and coupling a flight control mode are three separate functions. The ND draws a magenta line between flight-plan waypoints. That line can appear with either NAV receiver tuned elsewhere. The cockpit vertical navigation and roll navigation keys have no assigned click command. A visible route line alone is insufficient evidence of approach capture. See flight director and mode selectors.

docs.title: Transponder on VATSIM
docs.text:
Use the four-digit code assigned to your flight. With vPilot you can enter .x followed by a space and the assigned code. Copy all four digits, including a leading zero. Mode C and standby are separate from the code. Use the transponder mode control in vPilot to check which state the client is reporting. When a controller asks for IDENT, use the client's Ident control. This briefly highlights the existing return and leaves the assigned code in place.

Symptom Where to look The code is correct but the controller asks for altitude reporting Check the client's Mode C/standby indication. Re-entering the same code only changes the code field. A pedestal key moves but the client shows no change Use the client's supported transponder command or control and read back the resulting indication. The destination appears on the map after changing frequencies Compare the destination identifier with the simulator flight plan. Receiver tuning and route editing are independent.

docs.title: Axis Calibration and Troubleshooting
docs.text: With the H-60 parked, check each physical axis before adjusting how the helicopter handles. Open Controls, select the device, then open Hardware settings for that axis. Watch its input indicator as you move the control. Make a copy of your usual profile first if you're experimenting with response curves.

docs.title: Centre, direction and travel
docs.text:
1. Check the centre. Rest a spring-centred stick or the pedals and take your hands or feet off. If the indicator jitters, add a small centre dead zone and observe the same input again. Stop increasing the dead zone once the jitter disappears. A collective or throttle lever can rest anywhere in its travel and has no equivalent spring centre.
  2. Check each direction. Move fore and aft with the stick held close to centre on the other axis. Then repeat left and right. If the wrong axis responds, correct the assignment. If the correct axis responds backwards in the cockpit, reverse that axis.
  3. Check the ends. Move through the full stroke slowly. The indicator should change smoothly. A gap in the middle and a shortfall at the end are different problems. Compare the reading with the device's own calibration screen before changing the response curve.
  4. Check with all your devices connected. Move one control while leaving the others still. If the input jumps back to another position, inspect the bindings on the second device as well. This is easy to miss with a gamepad left connected beside a HOTAS.

docs.title: Common symptoms
docs.text:
What you see What to check Twisting the stick changes the nose direction even though pedals are connected Look for a yaw or tail rotor binding on both devices. Clear the one you aren't using in the active profile. Moving the quadrant changes a throttle lever while the collective stays put Search by that physical input and check whether it is assigned to helicopter throttle, collective, or both. The cyclic barely responds around centre, then moves suddenly Compare the physical input indicator with the response curve. A large dead zone uses up part of the available travel. A button changes the control a little at a time Check whether an increment or decrement command was chosen in place of an axis. A change worked yesterday but has disappeared Select the H-60 and check the active profile on the actual device. The stick and quadrant can each have a different profile selected.

For small adjustments, change one setting and repeat the same movement. Start with direction and range, then adjust sensitivity until small movements feel manageable with your stick length and grip.

docs.title: A bench check for a short-throw stick
docs.text:
Rest the stick at centre, move it a quarter of the way to the left, then hold it there. Repeat to the right and do the same on the pitch axis. Look at the response at rest, through the first part of the movement and at the held position. These observations answer three different questions.

Observation What it suggests Next adjustment The input wanders while the stick is untouched but holds steady once displaced Noise around centre Increase the centre dead zone just enough to absorb the wandering input. The centre is steady, but a small movement commands a large response on either side More response near centre than you want Soften the response around centre and repeat the quarter-travel check at both ends. The input turns before the stick does or jumps back when you hold the stick still Another axis, a repeated command, or a noisy device may be contributing Inspect all connected devices and any external control mapping before editing the curve. Both directions move together smoothly, but one endpoint is never reached Limited physical travel or device calibration Compare the two endpoints in the device's own input display. Recalibrate there if it also misses the endpoint.

A long cyclic extension increases hand travel for the same movement at the base. If you change from a short grip to an extended one, first try the existing response through a few small hand movements. A curve that suited the short stick can give a noticeably slower response after fitting the extension.

docs.title: Collective and pedal checks
docs.text:
Set the collective lever to each end, then stop halfway. Watch the in-sim lever or the axis indicator at all three positions. If the ends are correct but the middle is difficult to set, look for a hardware detent or a centre dead zone carried over from an airplane profile. Move away from that detent and back to the same spot to see whether it repeats.

For pedals, rest both feet lightly at centre and move each pedal through the same distance in turn. If yaw also moves when you use a toe brake, search for that particular toe input. Changing yaw sensitivity cannot remove an unwanted second binding. A centred stick and level helicopter need not give the same result in flight. The parked input check isolates the hardware from wind, trim and piloting assistance.

MSFS 2024 controller settings

docs.title: Cockpit and Cabin Lighting
docs.text: The cockpit has separate controls for backlit lettering, floodlights and the utility light at each seat. The cabin has its own colour selector. In a night flight, decide what you need to see first. If the lettering on the overhead is hard to read, raise the overhead backlight. If you need to see the shape of a switch or an unlit surface, use a flood or utility light.

docs.title: Panel illumination
docs.text:
Cockpit control or tooltip Area to watch OH PNL BACKLIGHT Overhead panel lettering INST PNL BACKLIGHT Instrument panel backlight LWR CSL BACKLIGHT Lower console, radio panels and collective lettering LIGHTED SWITCH INTENSITY Illumination of the lighted switches PILOT MASTER WARNING LIGHTING / COPILOT MASTER WARNING LIGHTING Master warning lighting on the selected side

The panel knobs above move in ten-percentage-point steps. One or two clicks at a time make it easier to balance adjacent panels. If the radios and collective labels are too bright while the overhead looks right, turn down LWR CSL BACKLIGHT and keep the overhead setting.

docs.title: Flood and utility lights
docs.text:
The cockpit floodlights cover a wider area. Their brightness knob has finer five-point steps. COCKPIT LIGHT COLOUR switches between the white and green floodlight effects. Colour and brightness are separate controls, so changing colour at zero brightness produces little to see.

Each seat also has UTIL LIGHT MODE and UTIL LIGHT POWER. Mode changes the colour of that seat's utility light. Power adjusts its intensity in twenty-point steps from off to full. If the other seat is lit and yours is dark, adjust the control for your side. This is a useful option when you want a little light at one seat without flooding the entire cockpit.

docs.title: Cabin lights
docs.text: The cabin switch has three labeled positions, WHITE, OFF and BLUE. View the cabin behind the seats to see the change. The cockpit floodlight colour selector and utility light knobs affect the flight deck, so they can be left where you want them while changing the cabin lights for a passenger view or screenshot.

docs.title: Night lighting from the pilot seat
docs.text:
1. Select the Overhead instrument view. Turn the overhead panel dimmer clockwise and look for the lettering around the switches to brighten. Turn it back down a click at a time until the letters are readable. The lettering circuit responds to the in-sim master battery, so a fully bright dimmer on a dark, unpowered cockpit is a poor test.
  2. Move to the Pedestal view and adjust the lower console backlight. The lower radio panels and the lettering on the collective share this setting. One is a good reference while setting up the other.
  3. Return to the pilot view. Use the floodlight if you can read lettering but cannot distinguish the unlit surfaces around it. Turning the flood knob clockwise increases its intensity. Choose a colour with the flood colour switch.
  4. Use the pilot utility light for a smaller illuminated area. Starting at zero, two clockwise steps give the utility lamp a 40 percent setting. The copilot lamp will retain its own setting. Finish by looking outside from the seat you'll actually use.

docs.title: When the lighting looks wrong
docs.text:
What you see Likely control or condition Lower radio panel and collective lettering dim together Both use the lower console setting. The overhead dimmer controls a different zone. Switching floodlight colour seems to do nothing Bring the secondary flood brightness above zero. Watch an unlit cockpit surface rather than a backlit label. Pilot utility light changes while the copilot's light stays dark Each seat has separate mode and power controls. Select the other seat's lamp. Cabin switch says BLUE, but the rear cabin looks greenish The switch tooltip reads BLUE while the selected lighting effect is green. Moving through OFF and back to BLUE makes the change easier to see. Multiple annunciators light together The TEST ANNUN control can illuminate the lamps for a test. End the test before reading individual AFCS or system selections.

When the aircraft loads, the time of day sets the initial lighting selections. The cabin, cockpit flood and utility lamp modes can therefore start in different positions on a daytime and a nighttime spawn. Read the controls after loading if you are comparing screenshots between flights.

Lighting and startup logic · Panel illumination · H-60 interior lighting controls · H-60 lighting circuits and effects

docs.title: Exterior Lights and Searchlight
docs.text: The H-60 has position lights, upper and lower anti-collision beacons, a landing light and a steerable searchlight. For a quick visual check, park near a patch of unlit pavement and use the external camera. It is easier to distinguish the two forward lamps when you can see both the fixture and where its beam lands.

docs.title: Position lights and beacons
docs.text: The position lights are red on the left, green on the right and white at the tail. Their selector is labeled NAV DIM, NAV OFF and NAV BRT. For the anti-collision lights, one switch selects UPPER, BOTH or LOWER. The other selects DAY, OFF or NIGHT. If one beacon is missing, check the first switch. If neither beacon is visible, check the second switch. The add-on uses different effects for the day and night settings.

docs.title: Landing light and searchlight
docs.text:
The cockpit has two individual push controls. Search Light CNTRL switches the steerable lamp. Landing Light CNTRL switches the landing lamp. When using generic lighting commands from a hardware panel, the searchlight uses the simulator's landing light channel and the landing lamp uses the taxi light channel. If your hardware switch operates the other lamp, try the labeled cockpit control to identify it first.

Four button assignments position the searchlight. The aircraft intercepts the following MSFS cowl flap commands, which explains their unusual names in a hardware profile.

Searchlight motion MSFS event Extend INC_COWL_FLAPS4 Retract DEC_COWL_FLAPS4 Left INC_COWL_FLAPS3 Right DEC_COWL_FLAPS3

The directional inputs move the fixture in small steps. With power available, extend the light several steps before checking left and right travel. At full retraction, the model returns the sideways aim to centre. If the lamp is lit but appears to ignore sideways commands, check that it has moved out of the stowed position. To confirm that a four-way hat is wired as intended, leave the helicopter stationary and move the beam across the same patch of pavement.

docs.title: Building a four-way searchlight hat
docs.text:
Use out and in on the fore-and-aft hat directions and left and right on the side directions. Start with only out assigned. With the helicopter parked and powered, switch on the searchlight and tap the assigned direction several times. Check for fixture movement in the external view, then watch the pool of light on the pavement. Once you can identify that motion, add the other three directions. Separate the command that switches the lamp on from the four commands that move it.

The model steps extension from retracted to fully extended and back. The left/right mechanism also has end stops. One press near an end stop may be difficult to see. Move it back towards the middle before deciding that the other binding is faulty. The model resets horizontal aim to mid-travel at full retraction. To repeat a sweep from the same starting point, retract, extend, then try the lateral input.

docs.title: Exterior light checks
docs.text:
Symptom Observation What to try in the sim A light comes on but the four-way hat seems ineffective The stationary landing beam is visible while the searchlight is dark Switch off the landing lamp briefly and identify the searchlight beam on its own. The searchlight extends but never moves farther left The lamp may already be at the left stop Tap right several times and then left. If neither works, recheck the two engine 3 cowl flap assignments. The pilot's view also moves The same hat direction is assigned to camera look Use Search by input on that direction. Move the conflicting camera assignment to a different control. A beacon changes from one fitting to two but still looks dark Lamp selection and power mode are independent Check the DAY/OFF/NIGHT selector as well as UPPER/BOTH/LOWER. Formation lights change but the red and green positions do not Formation lighting has its own rotary control Return to the nav selector for position lights. Its middle position is off.

The nav switch tooltips and the configured intensity values disagree at the two on positions. The tooltip labeled NAV DIM selects the higher output in the systems logic and NAV BRT selects the lower output. Compare both in the same light from the same external view when matching the brightness for a screenshot. The centre position switches the nav lights off.

docs.title: Helicopter Controller Profiles
docs.text: In MSFS 2024, select the H-60 at the top of Settings → Controls, then select your stick, throttle quadrant or pedals from the device list. Each device has its own assignments. If you select the stick while trying to bind the pedals, the pedals won't appear in the assignment you're editing.

docs.title: Four axes for the H-60
docs.text:
Physical movement Search term Assignment Stick forward and back Cyclic longitudinal Pitch axis Stick left and right Cyclic lateral Roll axis Pedals, or the twist grip on a stick Tail rotor Yaw axis Collective lever, or one lever on a throttle quadrant Collective Collective axis

Choose the continuous axis command for each lever or stick movement. Commands such as increase, decrease, left and right apply a step each time you press a button. An analog axis sends its position throughout the travel. A throttle quadrant works as a collective once you assign its lever to collective. The separate helicopter throttle command operates a different control.

docs.title: Where to save a binding
docs.text:
Use the helicopter category profile for the axes you want to carry between helicopters. Use the H-60 model profile for its special controls, such as the searchlight. For example, its searchlight uses commands labeled as cowl flaps in the simulator. Keeping those assignments in the H-60 profile leaves the same buttons available for other aircraft.

To keep a working preset, use the gear next to its name to duplicate it. A name like H-60 – twist grip or H-60 – pedals makes it easier to switch between the two setups. If you have both a twist stick and pedals, give yaw to the device you plan to use on this flight.

docs.title: Finding a command
docs.text: Set the filter to None when looking for an unassigned command. Assigned is useful once you want to review the bindings already on that device. To see what a specific physical input does, choose Search by input and move just that axis or press just that button. If a number appears beside a binding, open its gear to see the conflicting assignments.

docs.title: Example layouts
docs.text:
Spring stick and single throttle. Use the two stick axes for cyclic, the twist for tail rotor and the throttle lever for collective. Reserve one thumb button for rotor trim reset. A hat can take the four directional rotor trim commands if you use them frequently. Check the hat in Search by input before assigning all four directions. Many stock stick profiles already use it for quick views.

Cyclic, collective and pedals. Assign both cyclic axes on the cyclic device, collective on the lever device, and tail rotor on the pedal device. Toe brakes are two extra axes on many pedal sets. Push the left pedal forwards with your heel down, then press just its toe brake. Verify they register as different inputs before assigning yaw. A spare twist on the cyclic can stay unassigned.

Two levers on one quadrant. Decide which lever will represent collective. Leave the other clear while checking movement. Linking the handles mechanically while one still sends an engine throttle command can make the engine and collective controls move together. If the throttle levers and collective both move, search for the physical lever on the quadrant and check its assignments in each active profile.

docs.title: Hardware software and event IDs
docs.text:
Some bindings programs use an event name instead of the action shown in the MSFS menus. These are the four continuous inputs in the MSFS SDK.

Axis Simulator event Cyclic, left and right AXIS_CYCLIC_LATERAL_SET Cyclic, fore and aft AXIS_CYCLIC_LONGITUDINAL_SET Collective AXIS_COLLECTIVE_SET Tail rotor AXIS_TAIL_ROTOR_SET

If the hardware sends events through another application, switch off its aircraft profile briefly when tracing duplicate inputs. Search by input finds assignments made inside MSFS for the selected device. Commands sent separately by a hardware application can still reach the aircraft even when the MSFS search comes up empty.
